While the most topical question among educators is "How do we help students develop professional skills and competencies?", a few overlooked questions are "Are students really aware of the need for these skills? Could there be resistance to these skills? What underlying challenges would there be in helping them develop these skills?"

lessons.title: The elements of awareness
body: Before educators can effectively teach accounting students professional skills, they must address the awareness issue—both their own and their students. Students often don’t recognise the importance of these skills because they have been conditioned, explicitly or implicitly, to prioritise subject matter over professional development. Educators, in turn, must be aware of these challenges and how to bridge the gap between technical knowledge and professional competency.

When developing professional skills for accounting students, there are a few key factors to consider before getting into the specifics of what skills they need. The content of this discussion is based on my experience in course development, skill-building, and the challenges I’ve encountered along the way—challenges that may be useful to keep in mind for future skill development programs.
Three Levels of Awareness
Do students recognise the need for these skills?
Do they understand the practical implications of these skills for both academics and career success?
Are they aware of how lacking these skills could hinder their progress?
Are they aware of the practical impact of mindset (and other non-subject related concepts) on their everyday lives, their study habits, and approaches to situations both academic and profession?
We need to think of this on a few levels, at the very least, the conscious and unconscious.

The profession has been discussing the need for and importance of transferable skills, intellectual curiousity, the ability to adapt etc for quite a few years. There are unlikely to be students at higher levels in their academic journey who haven't heard of these, at the very least mentioned in their learning outcomes. So, students are probably consciously aware of these and the inclusion in their learning outcomes. Does this mean that they're 'aware' of the importance or challenges of these?

Unconsciously, many students don’t prioritise professional skills like communication or critical thinking because they have never been explicitly told to. Their prior education emphasised technical knowledge and subject mastery, leading them to believe that success is measured by how much information they know. They often fail to see the practical consequences of lacking these skills—until they struggle academically or in the workplace. In short - if their classes, lectures, assessment preparation predominantly focusses on technical skills, their assumption is probably that this is the most important thing. "Surely if these professional skills things were so important, we'd be covering them in class?".

I call this the 'in the corner vs in the classroom' challenge'. If their in-class lecturers are not focussing on these, then surely that means it's not that important. If it really was vital for assessments, then it wouldn't be a short course in the background presented by a non-lecturer, and the lecturers wouldn't just say 'go practice this yourself'?

There's also the difference between the acceptance that something is important and the daily implementation of this. Knowing that something is important doesn't mean that we work on this. Health and diet is a classic example of this. We know that it will be beneficial for our future health and longevity to have certain habits and avoid certain foods, but that doesn't mean that we actually do that. Behaviours like this often only become prioritised when the pain of staying the same is greater than the pain of change and sacrifice.

Thus, while there may be conscious awareness of these things, I believe the unconscious beliefs and behaviours aren't aligned with this. The question for us is how we integrate this into their teaching and assessment preparation and whether we prioritise them in meaningful ways.
Are educators aware of what students need?
Do they understand students’ perceptions of professional skills?
Are they conscious of the difficulties students face in prioritising these skills?
Are they aware of the connection between mindset (and other non-subject related concepts) and students' study habits, approaches to challenges and everyday life?

Even if an educator understands the importance of professional skills, they may not fully grasp the resistance students have toward them. Lecturers, having already mastered these skills, often assume their students will naturally develop them too. However, without explicit intervention, many students will not recognise the need for professional competencies until it is too late.
Challenges in Creating Awareness:
Even if an educator understands the importance of professional skills, how do they get students to prioritise them?
How do you convey that communication, problem-solving, and integration skills are just as crucial as technical knowledge?
Many students have been implicitly taught that subject knowledge is their primary focus. How do you shift this mindset?

It is not enough to simply tell students, “You need these skills.” They must experience and personally comprehend how the absence of these skills may negatively impact their academic and career success.

lessons.title: Excerpt what do i do
body: This is a short excerpt of a discussion with a postgraduate student whose firm has paid for her to obtain my support but she doesn't quite know what I do or how I can help her.

This starts framing what I do when I talk to students. Their perception is generally that mindset is similar to motivation. I’ve found that the best way to start the practical awareness of this is to discuss the work I will do with them in two categories: The practical study advice that will directly and tangibly improve their studying and the ‘behind-the-scenes’ issues that directly or indirectly impact their studying.

In the first few iterations of my coaching, I explained mindset concepts in more detail. While they listened politely and with some interest, students didn’t engage beyond that session because they couldn’t feel or see the direct relationship between what I was talking about and their next study session or exam. I found it was more effective to start the conversation using more practical, relatable issues they were currently experiencing and talking about these as part of the things we would deal with. They can easily visualise that if they have a mental block about a topic, they will struggle to study it, so this is a simple and quick example for them to start the realisation that there are things other than subject matter that may be impacting the effectiveness of their studying.

For this reason, the types of examples I give students of what I can help them with, often doesn't include classic mindset terms, since they're not aware of how these concepts impact their studying. Comfort zones, procrastination, self-doubt, stress levels - these are more practical, and I deal with them in terms of their relationship to mindset.

lessons.title: Example of study coaching session
body: The video below is a study coaching session I had with a postgraduate student. This is her first attempt at this level. She has failed some subjects in undergrad and is currently struggling with the workload, has anxiety and is panicking. She contacted me to help her with her study approach and anxiety.

It's important to note that she hasn't actually failed yet. She contacted me because this is the first year that she's started struggling to this extent. This is important because research often separates behaviour from the idea that students who have been, and are, passing clearly lean towards growth mindsets. This is an interesting indication that students can hold fixed mindsets in camouflage, given that she's at a postgraduate level.

My sessions are generally an hour. Since time is limited, we need to cover many concepts. This leaves a little less time for the type of interaction and feedback that formal research processes would prefer. Due to time limitations, I need to use subtle body language, vocal and facial expressions as cues to indicate whether I'm moving in the right direction.

While we cover a lot in the session, there will be follow-up discussions that repeat a lot of the material. The first session indicates that there is logic, hope, and awareness of how their beliefs and experiences are influencing their study sessions.

I give them one task to do when they leave: do questions first for a week. After they provide me with feedback (and if they actually do), we can work on more practical skills and address anxieties, concerns, etc. that arise from the process.

I've added captions to the video to help navigate the topics we cover. (The student has provided permission for me to use this video for these purposes. While I blur out the faces of most of the excerpts I use, I've left this video intact since some of the cues and reactions are less noticeable without the visuals.)

lessons.title: Coaching programme structure
body: There are three elements in my coaching programmes: Skills; Strategy and Mindset.

This is based on the concepts in James Clears' book 'Atomic Habits', in which he suggests that changing habits requires three levels: The habit itself; the strategy / processes that govern each day and decision; and underlying beliefs. (I explain it to students in this video)

The professional skills that curricula and exams increasingly emphasise are less tangible and theoretical than the subject matter. However, they still need to be taught, learnt and practiced. Students who have not used these skills before will be unsure about how to change what they do to develop these skills. My coaching is built on the idea that I may help them understand the importance of mindset and related concepts, but this alone is unlikely to have a practical impact on their learning since they haven't been given tangible processes to illustrate what these would look like, how to change from what they have been doing, and the possible challenges along the way.

I often start my coaching with the Skills component of the coaching, as this is the most direct connection to their studying and exam and enables students to see the practical benefit of the concepts I will discuss. Once they can see the practical gap, we can discuss how they study, the concepts they focus on, their goals when they study, what they aim to take away from each study session and their academic qualification (Strategy).

By acknowledging that the Skills and Strategy concepts we've discussed are new, strange and require change and a set of unfamiliar study habits, we can open the conversation to the Mindset elements - The beliefs about learning, comfort zones, sources of discomfort, existing habits and the underlying psychology of why all this happens.
The Connection between Mindset and Professional Skills
I've explained this in this video earlier in this course
Why do I connect Skills and Mindset so closely? Why can we not just include Skill requirements in exams and classes, without considering mindset?

In a domain such as accounting, where content and assessments have predominantly been theory-driven, where the focus in exams is on knowledge assimilation and application, professional skills represent very different dynamics. It is the shift in these dynamics that brings mindset into the discussion for me. A fundamental shift in expectations, learning, outcomes and requirements will require a certain approach to and belief about learning. Should this belief be inappropriate for the outcomes and skills required, students will struggle to focus on, implement and practice the necessary skills.

A big difference is the shift from a binary 'right or wrong' answer that can be learnt, to an 'appropriate' answer that needs to be built for the particular situation at hand. This shifts the student from a position of "If I've studied my work properly, I will know the answer to all the questions in the exams" to "Even if I've studied properly, I will still come across situations in exams that are unfamiliar and require me to build a solution from scratch. I will not 'know' the answer when I look at the question." If this student has experienced learning as 'right or wrong', with very clear negative consequences to being wrong (ie: failing assessments), this will reasonably be expected to have an impact on the ease with which they adapt to the idea that regardless of how well they've studied, they are still going to be in a position where they face an entirely new problem that they may struggle to get the 'right' answer for.

The comfort that students feel about approaching their learning in an 'every question has an entirely new, customised solution' approach can depend on their beliefs about learning and what good students should be capable of.

Content in this course includes videos I use for my coaching with students to explain concepts and skills, as well as excerpts from discussions with students relating to mindset and skills. These discussions and excerpts illustrate the connection between mindset, effective studying and professional skills.

lessons.title: Introduction to my skills and mindset work with accounting students
body: Students are very quick to jump to the solution, the practical tool, the steps and format, the tangible answer for their challenges. When it comes to professional skills, this means that their focus is on the quickest way to 'have communication skills'. While this is logical, it may also be ineffective if part of the challenge they're facing is mindset-related.

If a student leans toward a growth mindset, they are more likely to adapt, to spend the time, to practice the skills and are comfortable with getting things wrong and making slow progress. As educators, we can generally provide a few basics and processes for them, or at the very least, their tutorials and practice questions provide examples of what they're working towards. Someone with a stronger growth mindset will be inherently aware that this will take time to build, and whether they have a highly effective and detailed scaffold to guide them every step of the way or whether they have guidance that's slightly more vague, they're more likely to make progress - if for no other reason than the practice they put in and the small adjustments they make along the way.

To some extent, the very reason we need to find such specific, well-articulated, focussed and highly designed interventions to 'teach' these skills, is because students struggle to realise that the development of professional skills (or any new skills) is, by nature, messy, slow, gradual and often non-linear. This is a belief about how learning works, and thus connected to mindset. There are other skills that students require in order to learn, which don't seem to require the same consideration in terms of interventions, thus, it's not every part of learning, or every facet of studying - So, what's the difference?

My journey into mindset research began when I noticed a clear gap in students' academic performance, particularly in their study habits and exam results. I spent considerable time trying to understand the root causes of these gaps. It wasn't just about the content or the teaching method—something deeper affected students' engagement and learning.

Early in my teaching career, I lectured auditing at a private tuition center in South Africa where students were registered for accounting degrees at a distance-learning university. I taught second-year through to postgraduate-level auditing for both full-time and part-time students.

My classes included students with no work experience and those already in professional articles. Students often believe that if they have experience in auditing, their marks will be higher and studying will be easier, however, this was generally not what I found. Whether this was due to a complacency about the subject that led them to focus less on it in their study sessions, or that their work experience didn’t translate to academic performance as simply as people believed, is a question for another day. However, the takeaway for this discussion is that it wasn’t work experience influencing their auditing marks.

One constant stood out: students were generally reluctant about studying auditing. Before they started learning, they thought it was difficult and tedious, and exposure to the subject didn’t change this. I dedicated significant effort to simplifying concepts, and helping them visualise the concepts, better understand the work and have a greater comprehension of the topics and their application.

Despite these efforts—as well as practice tests, homework, in-class exercises—there was little to no improvement in marks. The students seemed to understand concepts discussed in class but struggled to translate that understanding into exam performance. Naturally, I took this personally, constantly interrogating, evaluating and refining my teaching approach, but the issue persisted. When I consulted fellow lecturers, their experience with the same students differed, which deepened the mystery.
A Key Discovery: Subject Matters

A breakthrough came when I started lecturing a third-year financial accounting class alongside auditing. The same group of students attended both classes. The contrast in their engagement levels was significant. In my financial accounting classes, they were enthusiastic, actively participating, and eager to tackle in-class problems. In my auditing classes, the same students were unresponsive, disengaged, and hesitant to attempt practice questions.
This revealed that the issue wasn’t me as a lecturer but something intrinsic to the subject. What made auditing more difficult and undesirable for students than financial accounting?

Over the years, I explored this more and found that the formulaic, calculation- and format-based nature of accounting was more comfortable for students, while they struggled with the level of communication and application needed for auditing - This is a significant skill difference. This difference was partially responsible for my students contradictory behaviour. With accounting, they had the format, the formula and the theory for the work, and so when I gave them a practice question, they knew where to start and what to do. They were in control, they knew that they had all the knowledge and the structure they needed to get to the solution. Auditing, however, posed a different challenge. They may know the theory, but every question looks different, it requires the knowledge to be used differently, and the answer to the next question may look nothing like the answer to the previous question. Worse, there's no 'formula' for sentences. You have to formulate the sentence in your head, including all the theory and terminology and the application and explanation into a nice neat sentence - This was a very unfamiliar skill for students who possibly chose accounting partially as a result of responding more positively at school to theory and calculations than communication. They didn't know where to start, they didn't have a structure or format, and their communication felt confused, was messy and took a lot of time to translate from knowledge in their head to a nice, concise sentence that looked even remotely similar to the markplan.

It wasn't so much the subject, as the skill requirements of the subject. I still hear from students that they're hoping that materiality calculations come up in their auditing exams. When I talk to them, they don't really understand materiality well enough to understand how and why the calculations are structured the way they are, but there's a calculation, and if they know the formula, they can plug in numbers, learn the 'if, then' rules and get enough marks to pass.

When I encountered the concept of fixed and growth mindsets, my initial impression was that I could personally relate to the challenges of a fixed mindset if I thought back to the difficulties I had when I was studying. I considered the challenges in light of the students I taught and wondered how these issues also impacted their studying.

My first application of this was a postgraduate auditing class I was teaching. I indicated that if they were struggling with their studying, I wanted them to stay behind after class and that I was going to chat with them about some concepts that may help them. About half the students remained after class.

I began by articulating some of the fixed mindset narratives, adjusting them for the studying they were doing. For example, mindset theory refers to whether people believe they can increase/change their intelligence. For my discussion, I phrased this as whether the students believed they would ever get to the point where they would understand difficult concepts they were currently struggling with. Mindset theory discusses performance goal orientation, whereas I phrased this as “The purpose of doing any questions is to get them right; there’s no point in doing questions if you know you’re probably not going to get them right". Mindset theory refers to effort belief as a fixed mindset students’ belief that the need for additional effort to achieve a goal may indicate lower intelligence; I phrased this as “Surely I wouldn’t be struggling so much if I was smart enough to pass this?”.

Thus, I was able to make the mindset theory concepts more personally relatable and reflect their study sessions and responses to challenging situations. I started with a discussion that some students may relate to these narratives, which would definitely mean that their anxiety levels would be higher. In that initial session, I was looking for some confirmation or denial of these narratives as an indication of whether their challenges mirrored the findings of fixed mindset students, or whether perhaps it was something I related to for my studying, but my students were struggling with something different.

What I was not expecting was the intensity of the reactions. There was a collective sigh or grunt of agreement for a lot of the narratives I mentioned, and as I continued, and discussed the possible impact these thoughts and feelings may have on their studying, quite a few students burst into tears. The prevailing feedback from the session was that I had articulated fears, emotions and anxieties that they deeply related to but had never put words to or consciously thought of. While I had not worked sufficiently with mindset theory to put theoretical concepts to these narratives, nor provide the tools necessary to help reduce these concerns, the starting point was clear to me:
There were some concepts from mindset theory that applied to their studying.
Mindset - Practical Application

While my starting point with mindset theory was to identify students' narratives and concerns, my practical purpose was to identify reasons for their reluctance to study logically, their resistance to questions, their discomfort with attempting questions, their fear of failure, their anxiety levels and their self-denigration when they didn’t learn something fast enough. I was concerned with how these mindset beliefs were impacting their daily study habits.

They were intelligent and committed to their studies - a student doesn’t get to postgraduate level by accident, and completing the undergraduate degree is confirmation that they can learn and display competencies at higher levels. So, how does this translate to postgraduate students who are terrified to attempt questions? I believed that if I could help reduce the resistance to attempting questions, they would be more likely to develop the skills they needed to pass. At the very least, the logical reality is that theory needs to be practiced. A student cannot expect to pass an exam if they have only studied the work theoretically, and have not practiced using that theory. If I could help them reduce their reluctance to questions, I could help them improve their marks.

Thus began my work with mindset and accounting students - The focus has always been on removing limiting beliefs and behaviours that are practically, and often unconsciously, influencing their study habits, emotions and academic performance.

lessons.title: Learning implications of fixed growth mindsets
body: Fixed and Growth Mindset Beliefs

While the table below provides theoretical explanations of these beliefs and their potential impact, I've included in this course excerpts from sessions I've had with students that provide a 'real-life' perspective on their thoughts and beliefs, I've linked some of them into the table. (These are lessons in this course with 'Excerpt' in the title)
Some theoretical beliefs:

If we compare the above beliefs to the study requirements of professional skills and exams discussed above, we can see that growth mindset beliefs are more appropriate. These students would be more likely to adapt to questions and problems that are subjective, require professional judgement, and are continually new and different.

Problems at higher levels require skills that cannot be learnt instantly (communication and application), this means that the student needs to be aware of, and comfortable with, the fact that no matter how well they know their theory, it will take some practice to get their communication skills up to the level they need, and that learning to apply their knowledge to different situations will take practice and exposure to new situations. This means that they will be getting questions wrong. They will take a lot longer to get from 'wrong' answers to 'right' answers. For a fixed'er, this can be stressful and contrary to their learning beliefs in terms of what 'good students' should be doing.

My coaching processes and Skills are designed on this basis. I scratch at the building blocks of beliefs, unarticulated and underlying concepts and skills required to develop professional skills and provide simple and tangible tools to help students begin developing these skills. Thus, the tools may not initially appear related to professional skills in how they are discussed in curriculum development. They may be perceived as oversimplified and inappropriate for the levels required in a professional qualification exam. Their purpose, however, is to provide scaffolds and starting points for students to develop growth mindset learning beliefs and behaviours, allowing them to develop the required professional skills.

lessons.title: Excerpt i feel stupid when i get the question wrong
body: An excerpt of a session with two postgraduate, fullt-time students. This was probably halfway through their academic year.

Their concern in this excerpt was how to deal with the feeling of stupidity they experienced when they attempt a question during their studying and they get it wrong / they don't know what the answer is. Their interpretation of this is that they don't know their theory well enough and are panicking that they won't be able to learn it all in the time they have.

At this level, their questions require higher levels of communication, application, problem-solving, all of which requires practice of using the knowledge that they may have. They may have perfect knowledge and still fail a question, because their communication and application is not good enough - This is the dilemma they are currently facing.
I discuss their beliefs about learning, and the difference between knowledge and skills. As you watch this, think of the Mindset Meaning System elements related to Fixed'ers:
Performance goal orientation - the belief that the purpose of learning is to get stuff right
Effort beliefs - "If I was smart enough to pass this, I wouldn't be struggling so much"
Helpless response - They feel bad, are losing hope and are avoiding practice questions out of a desire to avoid feeling stupid
Take-aways from this excerpt:
Their understanding of questions at this high level is still that they should 'know' the answer to questions as soon as they see it (The difference between 'problem matching' and 'problem solving')

At a postgraduate level, we would expect students to understand the cumulative nature of learning, deeper learning skills that build skills and develop understanding over time - yet their belief is clearly closer to "I should always know the answer to questions I look at"

There appears to be a fundamental misconception about what learning actually is - In trying to explain the difference in time it takes to memorise something vs learning a skill, I use the example of learning to drive a car. Note that the student who has not learnt to drive is surprised that having a memorised list of driving instructions doesn't mean that she will be able to drive. The student who has learnt to drive is aware that memorised instructions will not make it easier to drive... because she's lived through that experience. And yet, she has still not connected her experience of learning to drive a car, with any other learning situations. (Approx 4:50)
They believe that if you don't 'know' the answer to questions, it can only mean that you don't have enough knowledge and theory, and so they go back to theory (Approx 5:20)

lessons.title: The beginning of my mindset coaching courses
body: In this video I discuss the origin of my mindset coaching, and the first few iterations of the coaching concepts I introduced to my students. The first versions of my coaching courses made me realise the need for helping students develop a personal awareness of the need for growth mindsets and professional skills within their studying. They may logically agree that concepts like mindset and professional skills are valuable, but this is not enough to make any changes, or engage with content that is seen as 'outside' of exam preparation or subject-matter

lessons.title: Labelling students mindsets
body: Should we give students the 'labels' of Fixed or Growth Mindsets?

The very nature of mindset research goes against the idea of picking a label and keeping it for life. We change, adapt, progress and shift our whole lives. So, why am I continually 'labelling' students as fixed'ers or growth'ers?

When I work with students, one of my starting points is to scratch at whether they may be fixed'ers. This is not to try label and categorise them, this is to help me identify their possible study challenges as fast as possible. Some of those challenges aren't challenges that they'd identify for themselves.

They may diagnose their problem as 'not having enough knowledge to pass the exams', while my assessment may be closer to 'fear of attempting questions to practice applying your knowledge out of a belief that getting questions wrong is an indication that you may not be smart enough for this qualification.'

The underlying issue in the above example is their belief about how learning works (and if they hold this belief, it aligns with fixed mindset beliefs). It's not the 'belief' I'm interested in, it's the fact that if this is the belief they hold, they are more likely to display the following behaviours:
'hide' away in theory in order to avoid the risk of getting questions wrong, and in order to ensure high levels of mastery before attempting a question

have higher levels of anxiety because when you're studying, the risk of being wrong, whether in a study session or an exam, is a monster that lurks behind (and in front!) of every door, every single day

avoid asking for help because they feel that the reason they haven't mastered the work is because they're not smart enough, and because they worry what other people will think of them if they admit that they don't know the work

focus on calculation-style questions over discussion-style questions because calculations are always the same, as long as you have the formula and know what numbers to use, you know you can get the answer right. Discussion questions are always different and sentences are tougher to get right than sentences
avoid self-evaluation of prior tests and questions because they don't like the way that the failure makes them feel
focus their studies on answers over processes because their focus is on WHAT the right answer is, as opposed to HOW to build the right answer

All of these are practical implications and outworkings of this type of belief, thus I find it effective to ask a few questions that scratch at their mindset beliefs. From there, I can start the conversation of "Some students find that they struggle with xxx, how much or little do you relate to this...?".

I move from the mindset to the actions as fast as possible. In some cases, I don't use the word 'mindset' with them at all. I'm only interested in the information as far as it helps me identify what they're struggling with. If I feel that I can help them with their challenges without going through a mindset discussion, I'll move to practical discussions. In some cases however, their beliefs are tripping them up. They feel they're sabotaging themselves and don't know why. They are afraid, but don't know why. They're emotional and can't get to a point where they feel 'in control'. In these cases, I find that it helps to have the mindset conversation.
I use the 'label' for simplicity and brevity. My focus is on the beliefs, behaviours and failure responses that these two mindsets are generally associated with when it comes to their studying.

Mindset research incorporates more than 'just' the 'labels'. While mindset research in accounting education is limited to the evaluation of the label, mindset research itself goes further - A mindset meaning system. Mindset is suggested to impact academic performance through the mechanisms of goal orientation, effort belief and failure responses.

lessons.title: Generalisability of my work
body: Do all accounting students struggle with the issues I raise here?

The concerns regarding students' approaches and beliefs in relation to their studies do not necessarily apply to all accounting students. What portion of the student population would this type of work impact? This is a question I don't think we have the answer to, and there are a few things to include in our consideration of this. I discuss some of this at length as a reflection of the consideration I've given this same question, the impact of the possible answer, and experiences that (while not meeting the criteria of empirical evidence) provide insight that may go some way to either answering these questions or perhaps at least knowing what questions to ask.

Pass rates at higher levels in accounting qualifications may provide some insight into the portion of students who are the most appropriate audience for these types of discussions. The question would be whether the fails are related to issues raised here or 'something else.'
Is there research on this?

In a paper I wrote, I raise this question, using the pass rates of CPA, ACCA, CIMA at exit levels in 2024 and 2025 (The pass rate are around 45%). These represent the type of population we're talking about here - students who were able to successfully navigate earlier levels of their qualification, and yet cannot succeed at this point. This is an indication that there's 'something else' going on. My paper suggests a psychological rather than technical filter that may be an obstacle.

There is very little research on mindset in accounting education, and it is mostly skewed toward performers (i.e., not sampling students who have failed); thus, we only have mindset evaluations for students who are and have been passing. My paper takes non-mindset accounting research and considers whether the challenges raised in these papers may align to concepts raised in mindset research relating to fixed mindset behaviours - ie: Burnout, intention to leave, depression and seeking psychological help; confidence issues, perfectionism and identity; inappropriate study approaches; surface-level vs deep learning; external blame for failure; prevalence for 'spoon-feeding'; lack of use of interventional academic material and resources. This research is done in isolation, but if we consider these diverse issues through the lens of mindset research, we may see some underlying beliefs that may drive these various outcomes and challenges.

More research is needed in this area, specifically empirical research focussed on at-risk students. Accounting education research has a tendency to skew samples to performers, and often doesn't stratify findings according to performance, thus blurring the insights about whether these challenges are disproportionately experienced by at-risk students - and our question of cause-effect obviously cannot be inferred. (See the detailed mapping of Mindset accounting research here; and non-mindset accounting research here)

My work focuses on students who are struggling to develop the skills they need to succeed at their current level. This is mostly at higher levels of their qualification journey, and whether these students represent a small portion of accounting students, or a larger portion than we think, they still need support. Since this has not been explored within research or professional bodies, we do not have the answer for this.
The nature of the challenges I see my students facing drives the work I do, and this has changed

My student numbers have increased over the past 10 years, and my coaching programmes have shifted. These changes appear to be closely related to changes in exam outcomes. When I worked with students 10 years ago, the tools I provided them were somewhat different. The focus of my work has shifted over the years from more technical to more professional and mindset-related skills.

10 Years ago, when I asked students what their best and worst subjects were, I could bet that 90% of them would cite either Financial Accounting or Taxation as favourites, while struggling with Auditing and positively hating Financial Management. (I partially discussed my subject-related reasons for student differences in my discussion on why I started working on mindset). However, as the years progressed, I increasingly found that students cited Financial Accounting as a greater challenge. That then shifted again to Taxation - these shifts were closely aligned with shifts in exam questions shifting from calculations/formats/formulae to discussion-style questions (In the qualification path I was working with students on, Financial Accounting started asking for discussion questions on accounting treatment, and a few years later, Taxation started asking for explanations for deductions/inclusions in tax, and explanations of how calculations were done).

I keep connecting skills development challenges with fixed mindsets - if for no other reason than the fact that a growth'er is more likely to adapt to the requirements as they change. Change doesn't scare them as much; learning is learning, and increased time and effort spent on learning, or even changes therein, is not perceived as an indictment of their intelligence. The Awareness section of this course is designed with students who are more reluctant or resistant to change and are unaware of the impact of these changes - which aligns with the beliefs and habits of a fixed'er.
Higher levels of study are not comparable to lower levels

When we consider what support students need, we cannot exclude the differences in skill requirements and outcomes dynamics of different levels of study. If these levels were simply more complex or contained a higher volume of work but had similar question styles, requiring similar skills at a more advanced level, then we could compare them. This is increasingly not the case.

Students, for example, believe that the third year of their degree will ask the same types of questions, but they will just be 'harder'. In earlier levels, they may have been asked to perform a depreciation calculation with more 'simple' case-study details. In higher levels, they will obviously have more complex case studies with advanced calculations.

Earlier levels of study often require more memorisation of details and theory. If educators impart calculations and disclosures and then ask students to perform them in exams, students will develop learning skills to meet these requirements (Assessment guides learning). They need a good memory and the ability to remember calculations and plug the relevant details into those calculations and disclosures. (Thus creating a 'plug-and-play' learning style.) This does not mean that they're learning the core concepts of the topic, nor can we infer that they will be able to translate the skills they have practised (calculation, disclosure) to entirely new skills (professional judgement, application, communication).

When exams require new skills, students are most likely to continue applying the skills they have been working on until they no longer work. They are often unaware that it's not the 'difficulty' that has shifted; it's the underlying skill requirement. If exams now require discussion-style questions, will their memory and 'plug-and-play skills still serve them? If exams now require them to create a new solution for a problem they've never encountered, will their memory of previous solutions still serve them? Will their memory of what the theory says provide them with the answer?
This discussion is illustrated in a recording of a webinar I held with students

When we consider existing research on accounting students' study approaches, challenges, effort, and exam performance, it is important to keep these concepts in mind when we ask ourselves what the findings mean for us as educators.
Will at-risk students pass if they receive the same interventions and academic support as successful students?

When we consider research findings relating to successful students, it may be tempting to use these findings as guidance in terms of what we need to do more of for our students - If this is what's working for the successful students, then we need more of this to help our at-risk students.

Mindset research suggests that fixed'er students hold different beliefs, behave and respond completely differently to those with growth mindset beliefs. Simply put, we're dealing with two different types of people. What works for one group may not work for another.

This raises the question of whether at-risk students have fixed or growth mindsets. Simply having a growth mindset does not automatically equate to a pass in every exam, however it does mean that the student is more likely to respond to 'classic' academic approaches.

A question is whether our struggling students are growth-mindset students who are still in the learning process and not quite where they need to be at the point of their assessments or whether they are fixed-mindset students who may need a different approach to help them pass.
Existing mindset research in the accounting education domain does not specifically include students who are struggling or have failed previously, so this is currently unknown.
My work focusses on those who have failed or are failing

I work predominantly with students who actively find me, and they find me because they are currently struggling or have previously failed, thus most of my student population are at-risk students. What portion of total accounting students this represents, I cannot say.

What I can say is that in my experience, a significant portion of the at-risk students I deal with lean towards fixed mindset beliefs. There have been very few students who have sought my help who have growth mindset beliefs. (This is one of the first concepts I explore when interacting with students because it provides me with information about their study approach).
A valid question would be whether I just attract students with these beliefs (they may find my content on social media, and because they relate to it, they find me).

Do I find high ratios of fixed'ers in my coaching students because they're the ones that relate to my content? How many growth'er at-risk students are there out there who are looking for help and don't contact me because they're not struggling with the concepts that I discuss? What portion of total at-risk students would share fixed'er beliefs? Is it a big or a very small portion of the total failures - who somehow find their way to me?

I've pondered this question for a while. It doesn't make the work I do with the students I coach any less valuable since it reflects their challenges, but it does raise questions about the generalisability of my work.
A Case Study - Do the students who take my course represent a smaller, or a larger, portion of the total failures?

An interesting comparison arose in 2024 regarding a board course for failed students. I developed a board preparation course for this particular exam and have been running it for more than four years. Most of the students who usually enrol in my course are repeat students who relate to the concepts I discuss.

In 2024, unlike previous years, I was able to address the full cohort of students who failed the board exam in an online, live session organised by the professional body aimed at helping them consider their study approaches for their next attempt.

I split my presentation into two distinctive sections: Mindset and Skills. In the mindset section, I raised possible challenges they faced and felt (relating to fixed mindset beliefs and responses). In the Skills section, I focussed on the concepts that students perceive as 'exam technique' (Practical tools to help them answer questions, do discussion questions, plan their answers etc.). I structured my discussion this way because this is the work I do, however it also served a valuable purpose in identifying which of the two 'sections' students related to the most.

In the one-on-one sessions I had with students as they started the course, I asked them to consider the presentation I had given and which of the two sections made them feel that I could help them. This paved the way for a fascinating insight since there was a clear distinction between the Skills and the Mindset elements, and unlike previous board courses, they were not 'influenced' by my predominant 'mindset' messaging, website and content. I found that only a small handful of students indicated that it was only the Skills section that they had related to. The vast majority indicated that the narratives, emotions, study approaches and challenges discussed in the Mindset section were what made them contact me. I also asked whether they had heard of me before - the answer was mostly no. Thus their only impression of me was that particular session, and of the two sections I raised, it was the Mindset element that made them feel I could help them as opposed to messaging on my website, or social media. Some students indicated that they had heard of me, but thought that I focussed on 'motivational stuff'.

I record course engagement and notes for each student - Of the students I had one-on-one sessions with, I identified 85% of them as having fixed mindset beliefs to the extent that it would impact their studying.

A natural question here would be what percentage of students from the failure cohort took my board course in response to my presentation. This information is not available, as my course had a capacity of about 70 students, which was clearly communicated upfront. (I ended up taking on 100 students, as I found myself unable to keep turning students down who were struggling with their studying - this only represents 12.5% of the cohort.) The only answer to the question is that students contacted me almost immediately after the session, and I reached capacity within a week.

I connect the challenge of helping accounting students develop new professional skills with mindset challenges - By definition of a fixed mindset, these students will struggle to adopt new skills and processes.

I do not profess to know the percentage or volume of students who will relate to the challenges I raise here. We need more research to understand the approaches, beliefs and types of effort accounting students invest in their studies, especially in light of professional skill shifts.

lessons.title: Excerpt if this practice question was the exam i d fail
body: The excerpt of this discussion relates to goal orientation beliefs.
This student is repeating this level and is about three weeks away from their final exams.

At this level, we would expect that students have an inherent comprehension that their studying is intended to improve their understanding and learning, and that this is a gradual, cumulative process. Her belief however, is that she should be getting questions right.

Her belief is basically "If this practice question was the exam, I'd fail, and so I'm probably going to fail the exam". Interestingly, this fundamentally removes the element of 'time and growth' from the equation. She has no comprehension of the improving ability of practice, the impact of time and practice on skills and ability. In those moments, she only sees that what she can do right now, is all she'll ever be able to do.

Note the sense of enlightenment around the shift in purpose. My emphasis here is that this is a person who has a degree, has attempted this level before, and educators will mostly assume that a student at this level probably has the same perception of learning that they (the educator) has - And I feel this is a dangerous assumption.

lessons.title: What does mindset research in accounting education say
body: Research on mindset and its' impact on academic performance in the accounting education domain is currently limited and focusses on successful students
Surely there has to be more mindset research in accounting?!
I recorded a video showing the literature search I've performed to indicate how and why there appears to be more mindset research in accounting than there actually is:
This raises a few questions:
What would the findings of these studies indicate if students who are currently struggling to pass or have previously failed were included in these studies?

What portion of accounting students do these studies represent? Do these studies indirectly suggest that most accounting students are passing, and that's why the participants are mostly successful students? Or are successful students more likely to participate in these studies (Social desirability)?
The main takeaway from this is that research in accounting education doesn't say much about the mindset-related work I do. I hope that will change soon.
If we're looking to formal research to help us understand how mindset impacts our students, we'll have to wait until there's a little more!

People generally know just enough about mindset to recognise it and assume they have a more in-depth knowledge of the concepts and practical applications than they really do. Research that includes 'mindset' and 'growth mindsets' as keywords tend to imply that these are good things, important for success, etc., but don't go into further depth on HOW mindset is expected to create this success. There is generally a loose mention of the ability to learn and adaptability, but if we compare that to mindset research and the elements of the mindset meaning system that I've discussed earlier, we can see that these explanations lack some depth and breadth.

This means that people are more likely to dismiss conversations surrounding mindset because they are already accepted as positive. The biggest conversations at the moment revolve around how to improve and develop growth mindsets. But if we haven't explored mindset in more depth and truly understand the practical implications, can we expect any interventions to be effective and sustainable?

Khan et al. (2023) Undergraduate / Professional stream students (studying ACCA/CA)
Identity-based beliefs: Suggests students withdraw due to 'actual or pre-emptive failure' driven by entity theorist beliefs that circumstances are beyond influence.
Disengagement: Grit and resilience were negative predictors of academic burnout; low resilience was linked to withdrawal.
Mashishi and Rabin (2000) Fourth-year accounting students
(All students passed prior three years on first attempt; No data on pass rates)

Inappropriate learning strategies: Fourth-year students persisted with surface learning strategies despite the lecturer's expectations for deep learning; all students had passed the prior three years on their first attempt.
Molendijk et al (2024) Undergraduate students (Courses covered all three years of the degree)
Environment shapes goals: 'Assessment' was rarely mentioned for engagement/disengagement in non-assessed activities, suggesting goals shift when assessment pressure is removed.

Disengagement: Teaching material was the leading cause of disengagement (cited 'boredom' and 'too much information'); However, it was also the leading cause of engagement (cited ‘interesting’ and ‘detail’); Disengagement may be a helpless response, not an objective assessment of teaching material
Natoli et al. (2020) Second and third-year accounting students
Locus of control: >90% rated teaching quality/workload negatively, externalising responsibility; passive stance.
Inappropriate learning strategies: 91.9% adopted a surface learning approach - mirroring the ratings of negative perceptions of teaching quality

Environment shapes goals: Students prioritised "Assistance with examination techniques" (58%) over study advice or content, indicating a short-term performance focus driven by pass rates.
Smith et al. (2020) Undergraduate accounting students (Primarily second and third year)
Disengagement: Role stressors (ambiguity/overload) significantly increased burnout and intentions to depart the major; resilience acted as a protective mechanism.
Van den Berg and Rothmann (2024) Senior undergraduate students (Completed at least their first year)
Locus of control: Cynicism stems from a perceived ‘lack of efficacy and control’ over educational outcomes; feeling disempowered.
Disengagement: Cynicism was a strong predictor of the "intention to leave" the university; psychological detachment.

Abstract Could their study approaches be a result of mindset beliefs? They were successful students, why were they now using inappropriate study approaches?

Recent research into the quality of learning of accounting students has indicated that students lack requisite skills and competencies in a number of areas. Sharma (1997:125) refers to the following inadequacies, amongst others, that researchers have identified: That students approach accounting as memorisation and that there are significant declines in students' ability to handle complex problems. Wolk and Cates (1994:269) suggest that accounting students do not possess the 'broad intellectual, communication and interpersonal skills to tackle and solve unstructured problems using innovative methods. This observation is at odds with the university which values independent critical, analytical thinking. This study therefore investigates the approaches to learning of fourth year accounting students, and explores the manner in which students interact with the elements of the learning context (lectures and tutorials). The students' conceptions of accounting are identified. The results of the investigation into students' approaches to learning using Bigg 's SPQ inventory. revealed that the majority of the participants adopt a surface approach when studying accounting. At the same time the research showed that most of the students in the sample did not prepare for lectures, focused mainly on note-taking during lectures, and used tutorials to gain an understanding of concepts and principles (and not to develop problem solving skills). In addition, most of the students had a narrower conception of accounting than that promoted by the department. The results suggest that if accounting educators aim to develop the kind of accountants that will be able to cope with the demands of the business world, educators need to utilise research on students learning at tertiary level to improve their own teaching and the quality of students learning.

If we consider this study through the lens of mindset theory and my work with professional skills, we may raise the question of whether there are themes within their study approaches. Surface-level study approaches and the 'quicker' types of learning, theory-, memory-based learning, and using tutorials to learn the theory instead of focussing on problem-solving skills may be seen as learning approaches that fixed'ers would incline towards. These types of learning approaches get quick results and don't require 'sitting in uncertainty' and the time it takes to build competency.A student with a growth mindset would be more likely to develop the deeper learning approaches and focus on the skills that take longer to develop.A valuable element to add to this type of study would be why students adopted this approach. Should educators have more insight into students’ effort beliefs, they may understand why students choose their study approaches and would be better equipped to help them develop the necessary learning skills.
