lessons.title: The challenges of awareness
body: Knowledge is King - Students often value knowledge above all else in their studying. They believe they will pass if they have good knowledge of the subject. This may be reinforced by earlier education levels, where assessments focus on rote learning of theory instead of problem-solving. While this needs to be considered for the practical tools that will assist students in their development of these skills, the starting point is the realisation that their lack of awareness of this knowledge vs skills problem means that they will not focus on something that's not 'knowledge-based'. The challenge for the educator is to first find a way to impart awareness of this gap on a personal level.
A student’s awareness of their learning process is layered. When we analyse how students approach professional skills, we uncover key insights into what educators must address in course design.

For educators and professionals, the importance of these skills may seem obvious. We have developed them naturally through years of experience—on the job, through projects, and by navigating complex situations. However, the shift toward professional skills is not obvious for students who have come through an educational system that prioritises technical knowledge.
In traditional accounting education, the focus of their time in class, their academic content and assessments have been on:

Because of this, students may naturally assume that knowledge alone is the key to success. The idea that professional skills (communication, critical thinking, professional judgement, integration, problem-solving and application) are crucial only becomes evident when they struggle to pass exams that require more than knowledge.
Initial Awareness Questions and Challenges

Before their classes begin, students must have the mental space to ask a few questions: "Is the way I study going to get me where I want to go? Do I know where exactly I am going and what these exams will require of me? Have I thought about what my current study approach enables me to do, and what it doesn't enable me to do? Are there things I've avoided in the past that would have helped me? Do I need to make any changes to my studying that I may not have thought of?".

Assuming that these are natural questions that students will ask themselves is dangerous. In discussions I have with students, there are some common thoughts they have about what they should change in the future: "I need to spend more time studying"; "I need to do more questions"; "I need to work on my concentration"; "I need to work on xxx topic because I struggled with that last year"; "I need to stick to my study schedule more than last year.". While these are not incorrect or bad considerations, they do not touch on new skills, underlying challenges and the reasons why they weren't able to do these things before. (eg: They knew they needed to concentrate, stick to study schedules and do questions in the prior year, so why didn't they? What will change this year? What was preventing them from doing these things?). Their solutions to their questions are usually equally simple: "I need to stay up later and get to work earlier to spend more time on it"; "I need to work through the syllabus faster so I can get to more questions."; "I need a more detailed study schedule". - Simple, but unlikely to effect change. The underlying reasons why they haven't been able to achieve this yet is unexplored.

Once classes begin, these overarching, strategic-level questions are lost in the need to work through THIS topic as fast as possible. Students will revert to existing habits to prepare efficiently and smoothly for the next assessment that is already on the horizon. Their only obsession is 'the next test'.

These questions are especially important in situations where the next level of studies require different fundamental skills to the previous one. For most students I've worked with, they only realised that their questions were moving from calculation to discussions when it was too late. Their belief was that if they focussed on their theory, they'd be able to do 'anything' with it, and so to start with, they didn't pay attention to how the questions would be asked. They also are more likely to avoid engaging with what the exam may look like if they have a fear of failure or belief that you shouldn't look at questions until you know enough to answer them properly.

In most cases, students who find me have discovered this fundamental skill shift too late. Most of my students are those who have failed the year, often more than once. When we talk, the comments I hear are "I didn't realise how different it would be", "I thought it was going to be the same as the previous year, just harder", "I think that this level is just too hard for me, I don't think I'm smart enough for this", "I used to think I understood my work and I could answer questions, but now I can't answer questions so clearly I never understood my work".

Interestingly, the majority of students I work with do not consciously recognise that a significant element in their marks is their ability to communicate and apply their knowledge. They are not explicitly conscious that their most important area to work on to turn their failure into a pass is their communication or application. When I evaluate many students' tests, exams and prior scripts at all levels, I can see their knowledge coming through in their answers, but their application and communication are generally too weak to obtain the marks necessary. If they improved their communication and application skills, they could use exactly the same levels of knowledge and pass. (See: 'Is theory costing you all the marks?')

To pay attention to and make active changes to their beliefs and habits, students need to feel and comprehend the need for these skills personally. This needs to be as practical as possible. Generalisations leave room for socially desirable answers, the disconnect between logic and emotions and, if nothing else, the fact that they have not consciously articulated certain thoughts, anxieties and concerns. They may ‘feel’ them as they’re studying, but they haven’t necessarily put words to them, or they may have repressed them because they feel that they’re the only ones experiencing this, that their concerns indicate that they’re bad students.

My most effective approach is to verbalise the practical challenges, thoughts, and inner narratives students have that they generally don’t share or consciously voice. In many cases, they have never put words to or articulate for themselves. By verbalising thoughts that they’ve had, the initial trust that I understand them and can help them increases. Discussing these as challenges that I come across repeatedly among students decreases the feelings of isolation and the fear that there’s something wrong with them. In my case, I relate to many of these thoughts, as I experienced them myself, and the realisation that someone else struggled with these and is now qualified is a powerful element in their ability to believe their challenges will not stop them from qualifying.
Example: Illustrating the reasons behind avoidance of attempting practice questions (Learning beliefs; making mistakes)

lessons.title: Discomfort with uncertainty
body: As I taught and delved more deeply into the concepts that were challenging students, I tried to identify the underlying themes of their struggles. In the introduction to my mindset work, I mentioned that I taught the same group of students financial accounting and auditing and the value this had in comparing their engagement, performance, study approaches, and challenges. This helped me strip away subject matter and focus on the underlying concepts and differences.
Rules vs. Tools: Understanding the Fundamental Difference

I believe a distinct difference lies in the nature of the subjects. Financial accounting is rules-based. Once students understand a rule, they can apply it consistently—it's plug—and—play. ‘The process is predictable: journals, disclosures, formats, calculations—all follow a structured pattern.

Auditing, on the other hand, operates differently. It relies on conceptual tools and guidelines rather than fixed rules. Each scenario requires judgment and adaptation; students cannot copy and paste solutions. Unlike financial accounting, where numbers and formulae guide the process, auditing requires articulation—converting thought processes into words and justifications. This shift from structured formulae to open-ended reasoning created a significant barrier for students.
The Starter Problem - (Stepping into darkness)

Students appeared to fear making mistakes and lacked confidence in tackling unfamiliar problems with no distinct process, format or steps to get them started. If asked to "just try," they would freeze, unwilling to risk getting it wrong. They resisted, even with reassurance that errors were part of the learning process. While they were grateful to have me review their financial accounting attempts to guide them, they would not submit auditing work.

One of the biggest obstacles was students' reluctance to start practice questions. When I suggested we attempt a question in class to reinforce and illustrate the concepts we were working on, students in the financial accounting class were grateful for the opportunity to practice, and were noticeably engaged and positive about the process. When I repeated this approach with the same group of students in auditing, the response was markedly different. The reluctance to attempt anything in class was palpable. From taking a long time to find blank paper, to shuffling and struggling to settle, to staring at the blank paper for long periods of time, their reluctance was clear. When I walked around the class in the financial accounting questions, they would be working on the problems, perhaps interacting with those around them. In auditing, they left their pages blank, mostly waiting until the time was up and I would go through the correct answer with them.

I introduced a structured approach to substantive procedures to address the impact of a lack of format on their learning. I provided a simple formula, which I believe most lecturers use in some form: what, how, and why.
Identify the verb: What action is required?
Determine the document: What are you performing the procedure on?
What are you trying to prove? Why are you performing it? What assertion are you trying to prove?

With this framework, students had a starting point and a formula to guide their answer, and their engagement improved. However, while this helped them complete specific tasks, it did not foster their ability to develop independent problem-solving strategies across different areas of auditing. The underlying mindset issue remained unresolved. They were now more capable of substantive procedures, but not other topics. If I introduced similar formulaic approaches to different topics, they would improve. Topics that had no formulaic approach, remained challenging for them.

I felt this pointed to an underlying discomfort with ‘not knowing’ the answer when they looked at the question. If they did not have a clear format to follow, they would be required to create their own approach to start their answer. There could be no ‘framework’ of a solution in their heads until they created their own framework, and this meant starting to create a solution with a higher risk of error. Frameworks and formats that were learnt were less risky, and if remembered and used correctly, would be more likely to be accurate. However, creating or choosing their own approach was something they avoided. I refer to this as ‘stepping into the darkness’. With a format, you can step into a room that is already lit, you can see where you’re going, what to avoid, how to take the next step, where it will be. However, if you have to step into the room with no light, your steps are riskier, you need to find the light yourself, or navigate in the darkness. The fear of uncertainty, errors and failure are a lot higher.

A significant difference between auditing and their other majors (Financial accounting, taxation, financial management), was the requirements regarding communication. Auditing was still the only subject that required communication skills. Students were able to pass other subjects without focusing, or completely ignoring the communication-style questions. The exams were predominantly numbers-related - Journals, calculations, disclosures. A student could easily ignore a question requiring an accounting treatment discussion and still pass.

Reading students' homework submissions, their tests and exams, their struggle with communication was apparent. Their writing was not clear or concise and often did not convey the concept they were attempting to convey. They reverted to knowledge dumping, repeating theory where they needed to apply to specific situations, and they over-communicated concepts they were unsure of (ie: waffling). In discussions with them, their frustrations with ‘writing sentences’ were always raised. Their approach was often to learn the solution to a specific type of question, and then repeat the solution for other questions, which only increased the frustration when it was marked incorrect, since it was irrelevant in the following scenario.

The level of challenge facing students in auditing related to communication, which was not an issue for other subjects at the time, was one of the reasons I spent more time searching for tools, skills, and approaches that would assist them in translating the theory they were studying into answers that met the objectives and appropriately applied and communicated that theory.

While auditing marks generally trailed behind those of their other majors, as the years progressed and more discussion-style questions were introduced into their other subjects, these marks also started decreasing. Students could no longer ignore the communication elements of their subjects, and they struggled to translate their rules-based learning into discussions. Thus, it was clear to me that the problem was not auditing as a subject but their underlying communication challenges, which were impacting their marks.
Underlying theme: The Chair (Sitting in Uncertainty)

There is a common theme if we consider the abovementioned concepts (Rules vs Tools; The Starter Problem; Communication challenges). The theme is discomfort with uncertainty and an absence of pre-defined structures. While this is more obvious in the case of Rules vs Tools and the Starter Problem, this is a little less obvious with communication.

If we oversimplify the requirement of discussion questions, we find ourselves with a requirement to create sentences, with words in different orders, sentences in different orders. The sentences cannot be learnt and re-used in different scenarios. In every question, the student needs to think of the shape of the answer as a whole and what they want to convey, then break the bigger picture down into various sentences - There is no format for this. From there, they need to put the sentences in a coherent order that will build their discussion in a logical manner - again, no predefined format to use. From there, each sentence must be chosen and broken into words that will convey that element of the discussion, including both theory and application - again, no predefined format. Thus, the student is required to create a set of sentences with no formulae to tell them where to start, what to do next, how much or little to do, and what it should include.
I use a picture of a chair embedded with shards of glass as an illustration of the feelings of discomfort students have with ‘sitting in uncertainty’:

When I work with students, I show them this picture and ask how much or little they relate to the idea that this is what doing practice questions and tests feels like. An overwhelming majority of students relate heavily with the picture (in some cases adding that it also feels like the room is on fire as well!). When I discuss this with them, I indicate that given the discomfort, it would be natural that they would avoid sitting in The Chair, which translates in practice questions to stopping their attempt, reverting to theory or the solution and not persisting in finding a solution themselves.
They want the answer - they do not want to sit in uncertainty, it’s too uncomfortable.

lessons.title: Introducing the cold
body: I found this a great analogy to help students visualise that there are concepts that impact their performance that are not directly connected to the task. They often interpret things that they struggle with and can't articulate as "... there's something wrong with me in some way. If I was studying properly, I wouldn't struggle with this.". Using the analogy that a climber will struggle with the cold, no matter how fit they are, conveys this message more effectively than other methods I've tried using before. So, I often talk about the work I do with them as "Let's get you a jacket!"

lessons.title: Survey responses what are your challenges
body: When I start working with students, I ask them to answer a questionnaire that helps me obtain some background information and understand what they need help with.
One of the questions I ask them is what they feel is their biggest challenge that they're hoping I can help them with.
This question helps me understand what they're struggling with, and it also provides valuable insight into their own assessment of what is most likely to get in the way of their success.

Over the years, I've also learnt not immediately address the issues they raise. They may be a good starting point, or they may be a misdiagnosis. When I work with students, I have one-on-one sessions with them after these surveys, so I have their responses in my head as we talk. This allows me to scratch a little more at their experiences, challenges and practical study approaches.
Responses from prior courses

The responses for this questionnaire came from a group of students who were studying part-time, working at an audit firm who provided my support for their students. 90% of the students in the group were studying at postgraduate level, with a small handful still completing the final year of their degree. (They were studying through various educational institutions). These questions are open-ended in order to get their impressions as opposed to lead their thinking.
The narratives in some of these responses provide a lot of insight into their frustrations, emotions and beliefs.
The green highlights represent students who identified as part of, or their main concern, issues relating to Skills or Mindset.

Note: 'Exam Technique' is the most common way students refer to their ability to 'answer questions the way examiners want to see. For them, this includes communication, application, reading and interpreting the question. (Basically, anything that relates to how to answer a question is considered 'exam technique')

I've separated the student responses between the amount of exposure that they've had at the current level of study. This is important for me because a student attempting this level for the first time may base their perception of their challenge on what they struggled with in the prior year, or what they're hearing from others who have attempted the level before. Their challenge may not relate to the level they're about to attempt, since they've had no exposure to it (Thus there may be a disconnect between their self-assessed challenge, and the challenges they're about to face that they haven't encountered before.)

Students who have had previous exposure to this level provide insight into students who have tried this, and their self-assessment is based on what this level requires. I would expect that these students would identify different challenges to the first-timers, since the level and skill requirements are different. (This is true of the levels in this particular survey as it represents the difference between undergraduate and postgraduate levels). Yet, most of the challenges identified remain the same.

I generally find that students attempting the level for the third time (or more) are more likely to shift their self-assessed challenge away from the 'usual suspects'. The results below bear this out, and while this survey is not empirical evidence, it does reflect the trends I find. Students seeking out mindset and skills coaching are generally attempting their level for the third time.

It seems to be the trend that when they fail the first time, they diagnose the problem as the 'usual suspects' (Not understanding the work enough, not enough time, technical issues). This is what they worked on addressing in their second attempt. When this doesn't work, they start looking at alternative issues.

The students in this questionnaire are part-time students, so it is both expected and valid that their major concern is time management. Calling their 'time' challenge a 'usual suspect' does not mean I feel this issue is irrelevant.
Time is most definitely an issue - My question for my students is: What are you spending your limited time on?

lessons.title: In class vs in the corner
body: Separation between Mindset & Skills and Classes

In the past, I have run Skills, Strategy and Mindset courses (Including the mobile app, on-demand courses as a library, and one-on-one sessions with students) alongside the syllabus for educational institutions. No matter how practical, incremental, short, accessible and convenient the content was, the engagement was low, with the predominant feedback being, “I don’t have time for this with the work given to us by the lecturers for our next test.”

It was always seen as a ‘motivational’, ‘nice-to-have’ course in the corner of the room that wasn’t as important as the subject matter. If lecturers do not incorporate this into their subject-matter teaching, students will interpret it as unimportant and deprioritise it. When lecturers, at the very least, directed students to my content, indicating the practical connection between the content and their ability to pass their exams, the engagement was higher. Students trust in the ability of the lecturer to direct them to what they need to do to pass will surpass other messages.
We know the main question in most students' minds: "Will this be in the exam?"

‘Do as I do, not as I say’ is a powerful concept that applies here. Educators may continually emphasise the need to practice these skills, fail questions, and consider non-subject matter issues. Still, if they are not prioritised in class, the student implicitly receives the message that these are not as important. Surely, the purpose of the class is to deal with the most important things that will be most relevant to my exam and my abilities." and "These skills cannot be that important if my lecturer is not spending time on them." Lip service may be paid to these skills within these classes, but the implicit priority on the importance of concepts is imparted by the educator and the time they spend on them in class. ie: “If communication skills were really as important as the formulae, then the lecturer would be covering it in class.". "They say it, but then they say it can be worked on in my own time, so clearly, it’s not as important and can’t be that tough.”

Ideally, these Skills should be integrated into students' subjects, in order that students can experience the impact and essential nature of these skills. Having a separate 'communication' class, for example, can create the impression that communication is somehow separate from their subjects and topics, otherwise they would be included within the classes - and if there is no direct assessment for that class, there will be no prioritisation on the application of that content. If communication skills were required to pass the tests, they should be covered in class. Since they're covered in a separate class, with no practical or direct connection to the next test they're writing, students' emphasis and focus will most likely be on their next test. They will deprioritise whatever is outside of these requirements. Eg: Financial calculator skills would not be run as a separate class, because they are needed within the studied topics. Questions can't be answered without the skill of using financial calculators, so they need to be incorporated within the topic and classes, students learn the skills as they work with the content. It's part of their learning, not an aside.

An interesting results comparison was a programme I ran with an educational institution. The programme included all the elements of my coaching (Mindset, Strategy and Skills). It was designed to help them assess their study approaches, consider the requirements and outcomes of their exams and make necessary changes to their study habits and focus; providing support and awareness of where their challenges and anxieties were coming from; providing practical tools to improve their next study session and practice questions and exams regardless of what topics they were currently working on; and personal engagement with myself for support, motivation and advice.

When the programme was run 'in the corner', there was very little engagement and a minimal impact on pass rates. When the programme was run as an explicit part of their courses and included in their study schedule, their pass rates increased by 15% on the prior year.

I provided full support (Including the mobile app, on-demand courses as a library, and one-on-one sessions with students) for their students for the duration of the year. Included in this were monthly sessions for lecturers to attend in order to understand what I was giving their students and how they could support them and direct their students' attention to relevant content on a regular basis. The results were disappointing.

Through the course of the year, there were students who engaged with me, felt progress and continued to engage. Some students 'found' me much later in the year, as they started panicking about their ability to pass and decided that ANYTHING was worth trying.
This programme was another tough lesson in the importance of and the challenges surrounding the students' (and lecturers') awareness of the importance of non-subject concepts and skills.

My challenge here was that they simply could not visualise what I was going to help them with. In order to help them visualise this, I needed at the very least, some session or engagement that would allow me to illustrate or explain this. Their overall impression was "This is a motivational, warm/fuzzy thing I don't have time for."

As soon as their classes began, their attention was entirely focussed on their subjects. Trying to pry their mental energy away from the technical topics for long enough to understand how something that was not a lecture could possibly help them pass was challenging. As a lesson I've learnt from this, I now insist on having at least two compulsory sessions with students BEFORE their classes begin. This allows them to focus on how they plan on approaching their studies before they dive headfirst into the topics without a clearly defined idea of how they will structure their studies and their challenges, given their past experiences and future challenges. They also have the mental space available to pay attention to how something that is not subject-related may assist them.

From the beginning of the course, we agreed that we needed lecturer buy-in. A simple solution to partially address the awareness challenge was for lecturers to actively point students in the direction of the content in the programme (mainly at the beginning of the year) to increase the initial engagement and help students experience what it was that I did and how it could practically assist them. The impression created by the simple inclusion of the programme concept within their class was enough to make students feel that there may be some connection between their studying and what I was providing for them.

Lecturers had access to the same mobile app the students had, and the agreement was that at least once each week (at least for the first 6 weeks), they would actively direct students in their classes to a specific piece of content in the app. They didn't need to repeat the content; they just needed to 'point' something specific out to the students as something that would help them.

While the lecturers initially bought into the course and concepts and agreed that the concepts (especially the Skills that would directly impact their practice questions and exams), attendance and engagement in the lecturer sessions were disappointing. Within their schedule, they simply didn't have time to spend on this. It was deprioritised and allocated as a 'nice to have' they couldn't spend time on.

I provided lecturers with access to the same mobile app as the students in order that they would be aware of the skills and advice I was providing students with and provide me with any guidance, feedback or content they wanted to add, adjust or discuss - There was no engagement in this process. For the most part, the lecturers didn't download the app or go through any course contents - Which means they were not mentioning this in their classes.

In classes where the lecturers actively encouraged students to download the app and engage with the programme, there was a higher level of engagement in the programme. The feedback I received from new postgraduate students was, "My lecturer said this is really going to help me. I don't really know what you do, but he said it's important, so here I am". When I contacted students who had not engaged, the predominant response was that they didn't have the time or didn't need my help (their pass rates, however, indicated that they were not performing well).

lessons.title: Survey responses do you feel reluctant to attempt questions before and after course
body: How does the fear of 'being wrong' impact study habits?

If a student has learnt that you should 'know' your work before you attempt questions, if they've been explicitly or implicitly taught that knowledge should come first, they are left with a feeling that you need to know all your work before you attempt a question. While this seems logical, one of the challenges is this:
How do they 'know' whether or not they 'know' all their work?

They will wait until they 'feel' they know their work well enough - This means that they base their study approach on feelings as opposed to logic. They do not realise this is what they're doing, because it has made sense, and been effective in previous years.

This approach is easier at earlier levels in their studying, where the workload may be small enough that they can work through the syllabus to the extent that they feel they should and where they can obtain the levels of knowledge and competence for each topic before moving on. Assessments at earlier levels may also feed into this approach - If the questions are closely related to the theory, then once you know your work, you can answer questions.

In later levels, the volume increases, and so does the application level. No matter how well they know their work, they have never applied it to 'this' situation, which means that they won't 'know' the answer immediately. Based on their previous study experience and beliefs, they believe that this means that they don't know enough of their work, and so they revert back to theory.
A common challenge is "I'm not ready to attempt questions because I don't feel like I know my work well enough"

In later levels of studying, they will never reach that same level of feeling competent, if for no other reason than the fact that the application and problem-solving requirements mean that they will never have seen 'this' question before and will thus not 'know' the answer.
Feedback from a Board Course

The table below reflects feedback from an exam prep course I run for students who are preparing for a Board Exam (IAC - Initial Assessment of Competence) For context, these are South African students working towards their Chartered Accountant qualification with SAICA (South African Institute of Chartered Accountants). All these students have a postgraduate qualification, majoring in Financial Accounting, Financial Management, Taxation, and Auditing.

These are students who have already passed a postgraduate qualification that many students cannot pass. This means that they have a high level of knowledge and have managed to pass exams set at a high level. They have been studying for at least four years. This often creates the impression that they would by now be comfortable attempting questions, that this would be a natural part of their study approach - their narratives indicate otherwise.

Many of these students have unsuccessfully attempted this exam before (Attempt # indicated in the first column), and yet they are still not comfortable attempting questions. Their previous attempt at this exam is no more than six months ago, thus it should not be long enough to warrant 'starting over'. Educators may feel that since they have attempted this exam fairly recently, they should be comfortable starting with questions to assess where they need to focus their attention. This is generally not the case.
I interacted with these students as they started my course and got an impression of whether they generally avoided questions or were comfortable attempting them.
After the exam was over, I gave them a survey to get some feedback.

Of the 29 students listed below, only six indicated they were not reluctant to do questions, and two of those students had already worked with me, while one of them appears to contradict herself. Thus, only three students appear to inherently have a comfort with approaching questions

- The green highlights represent students who explicitly indicated that they were comfortable with doing questions, and their feedback supports this. - The student in red is a student whose feedback contradicts her first response. - The students in orange are students who have worked with me before and so they have worked through their discomfort and question avoidance in previous years.

lessons.title: Conscious vs unconscious beliefs the disconnect
body: Suppose there is a disconnect between students' conscious beliefs and their unconscious beliefs and instinctive responses. In that case, they may disengage from discussions explicitly relating to beliefs that they already feel they possess. Eg: If students believe they have a growth mindset, then giving them a session on growth mindset development will be less relevant for them and they are unlikely to engage with any depth.

In my experience, yes. This is not merely a 'social desirability' issue. In many cases I've dealt with, they are happy to be authentic and honest, but when asked 'theoretically' what their beliefs are, they respond as growth'ers, and believe they hold these types of beliefs. When we scratch further at their daily behaviours and responses to specific situations, their responses, emotions and narratives reflect a disconnect.

This student approached me for help with one of her third year Auditing subjects. Within the discussion, we chatted about her career choice. While she had overcome some challenges relating to her studying and believed that this had helped her develop resilience and a growth mindset, as we started scratching at her choices a little more, the disconnect between her conscious and unconscious (or perhaps just unarticulated) choices became more apparent.
Example: Webinar poll of third year accounting students

I ran a free webinar for third year accounting students studying through a distance-learning university in South Africa. The webinar was focussed on study habits and strategies, in line with the mindset and strategy coaching I do. At the beginning of the session, I ran a poll asking four questions.

The first two questions were paraphrased from the Implicit Theories of Intelligence Scales (ITIS - The most commonly used mindset evaluation tool). Question three and four were examples of narratives that students may have in specific study situations.

These students registered for my webinar because they were struggling, and had no incentive to answer in a specific way, they were aware it was an anonymous poll. Their responses are interesting in their contradictions. The 'theoretical' mindset beliefs that they consciously feel they hold, do not appear to translate into either emotion, instinctive responses or beliefs in the moments of 'struggling' with learning. 100% of the answers for the mindset questions reflect growth mindsets, yet very few responses relating to actual situations reflect growth mindsets.
Example - Mistakes vs Being Wrong

In this coaching session, we discussed the students' avoidance of doing questions. She agrees that she needs to do questions to pass, but struggles to do them. Our discussion related to her negative association with the idea of being 'wrong'. However, her conscious belief is that making mistakes is a positive thing.
Unconsciously, she believes that being 'wrong' in her studies is not the same thing as making a 'mistake'.
Implications for educators?

Generic mindset and professional skills training may not be effective. Over the years, I have run mindset courses and sessions discussing mindset and skills as 'generic' issues, talking about them in general terms, and by necessity, outside of their subject-matter classes. This was largely ineffective, and I believe that the disconnect above is partially responsible for this.

This led me to using more specific examples, narratives, illustrations of situations that students face and experience. Once I started articulating situations they practically find themselves in, they could relate better to the beliefs and narratives I was referring to, and this opened the door to their engagement. (The psychological 'hook' I referred to earlier).

This is as relevant in the awareness phase as it is in the practical, skills-based phase. Giving students vague, generalised solutions to develop growth mindsets and professional skills may be ineffective. As much as they are unaware of the beliefs they instinctively hold, they are unaware of the specific steps to take to change this in their daily lives. Generic growth mindset advice may include: "Be ok with making mistakes." But if you've always worried about what mistakes mean, if this is a deeply held concern for all the reasons mindset theory suggests, how does one simply 'stop worrying' about being wrong? How do you just forget all the embedded and habitual beliefs, instincts and responses and shrug these off in favour of enthusiasm over getting things wrong, failing practice questions, asking for help, and generally feeling 'stupid' through the learning journey?

lessons.title: Excerpt making mistakes vs being wrong
body: This excerpt is another example of the 'hook' I use to try and help students identify their unconscious beliefs, as well as the disconnect between conscious and unconscious beliefs.

In this student discussion, I was talking about the students' avoidance of doing questions. She agrees that she needs to do questions to pass, but struggles to do them. Our discussion was relating to the negative association she has with the idea of being 'wrong'. However, her conscious belief is that making mistakes is a positive thing.
Another interesting element of this chat was her comment about the perception of the industry (around 1:30) - See under the video for an additional discussion on this
Unconsciously, she believes that being 'wrong' in her studies is not the same thing as making a 'mistake'.
The profession is supposed to be 'smart'

At about 1:30, the student mentions that part of her anxiety is the feeling that people expect that she should get things right, because "you're supposed to be smart...". This is definitely something we as educators can address. We know that this is a perception that people have of the profession, and we need to be aware of the impact on students. They're exposed to lecturers, audit partners, successful students, all of whom discuss their successes, and may even mention their challenges, but the focus is on SUCCESS. ie: BEING SMART.

I feel we need to have more conversations with our students about things that we STILL struggle with. They need to know that learning IS continuous. That the smartest person, when learning something new, becomes 'stupid' again. That passing an exam, doesn't mean you know everything and should be able to answer everything. They need to see authentic lifelong learning in action... which starts with "There are things I still don't know... even though I'm qualified. I have NO idea how to..."

I ran a mindset webinar on 'Procrastination' for a group of PhD students from various disciplines. Their responses and challenges mirrored this discussion above. Part of the discussion was around why they were struggling to make progress in their research. When we got to the point of discussing the perception of 'smart', there was a clear resonance in the group: "The people around me, my supervisors and professors are all smart. They know the answers to everything - and that's what 'smart' looks like. That's what I'm supposed to be... and I'm not. So I'm going to hide away until I know exactly what to do"

It's a completely logical concept that someone learning to do research will struggle with steps along the way, that's the entire purpose of learning to do research, and yet, regardless of this logical messaging, of support, of available resources, the inherent feeling that they're 'supposed to be smart' pervades their behaviours.

lessons.title: Lifelong learning what does this look like
body: A student's perception of lifelong learning is most likely to reflect the learning they have the most experience with and the idea that they will continue to do this for the rest of their careers. What does this mean for them? What are students visualising? Does this match the visual that the profession has in mind when referring to lifelong learning? If these two visuals are not aligned, then discussions of this and skills and processes designed to develop it may be ineffective.

A student whose learning experience is in a traditional education environment may have the following perception of learning: They will be told what they need to learn to achieve the desired level of competency. They will be given or taught the knowledge. Once they've understood, mastered, and practiced the types of problems the knowledge will be used for, in which they are able to obtain a majority of the points on the suggested solution, they will then have 'learnt' the work. This will be assessed through a formal examination of these concepts. Passing the exam validates the learning and that they have achieved the required level of competency.

What is this student's vision of lifelong learning? They will continue to enrol for or take training courses in which they will be given the knowledge they need for the following work they will be required to do. There will always be suggested solutions and pre-defined competencies against which to measure. They will be expected to learn what they're told to learn at the levels they're told. They can practice their knowledge and skills before it 'counts'.

What is the profession's vision of lifelong learning? Professionals must identify skills and knowledge gaps relevant to the work they are currently involved in or intend to pursue. They must find, learn, and assess their knowledge and skills. This may be formal training courses, personal research (Google, ChatGPT, talking to colleagues, reading, etc.), and considering how it would be applied to specific situations. There are no practice questions; there are no suggested solutions. They will be required to develop a solution for an unforeseen problem, possibly without having anyone validate the accuracy or appropriateness of the solution they have created. In an everchanging environment, with new technology, societal shifts and expectations, they need to be comfortable with the process of taking existing knowledge and applying it to new situations quickly, and close knowledge gaps along the way.
The student and the professions' vision of lifelong learning do not align.
An unarticulated, underlying characteristic - Uncertainty

The profession requires its members to be lifelong learners, partly as a reflection of the constant changes to technical, societal and environmental circumstances and knowledge. What does this look like for a student? Doesn't the fact that they've registered for the course mean they are already lifelong learners? Growth mindsets are generally linked to lifelong learning as a natural reflection of the belief that learning is valuable and the acknowledgement that learning is essential and will continue throughout life. Mindset research suggests that mindsets impact the type of goals that people choose. This is often interpreted as "People with a growth mindset will choose more challenging career goals". Accounting professions are generally perceived as challenging, and thus, accounting students may consider themselves to have growth mindsets purely because they chose a challenging qualification path. This is a highly oversimplified interpretation of mindset research. Growth mindsets are indeed intrinsically connected with lifelong learning and vital to the development of this trait, however, the belief and goal orientation at the heart of a growth mindset and lifelong learning is comfort with uncertainty and the ability to step into problems while knowing that the answer either doesn't yet exist, or that they don't yet know the answer themselves.

Implicit in the concept of lifelong learning, or an often unarticulated, underlying skill, is comfort with uncertainty and continuously taking on projects, topics, areas, jobs, problems, and functions that require the professional to start at zero. This is very different to learning a subject where the material is designed to impart the knowledge first and only then start solving problems. This is not a reflection of uncertainty, of self-development, of self-learning. This suggests that the professional would not attempt a project until they have done specific training for it, studied it, and covered all the theoretical, technical and skill requirements before attempting problems. An important element of lifelong learning is the ability to deal with uncertainty, and developing a working relationship with the feeling of 'not knowing...'. This is not a comfortable concept for a student who has been taught through the 'Impart, Learn, Solve related problems' process. A practical illustration of lifelong learning within studying is simply the students' ability to attempt questions for a topic they have not yet mastered or perhaps have not yet learnt.

While this is an oversimplified version of lifelong learning, if a student is unable, or too uncomfortable, to attempt to solve an academic problem in preparation for a test when they are not entirely comfortable with all the concepts, they are not likely to become professionals who can face and embrace situations where they do not have all the knowledge, skills and experience before they attempt the project. An unarticulated skill necessary for lifelong learning is comfort with uncertainty and the ability to start, or try to start, solving a problem while they still don't know the answer. Helping students develop the practical skill of attempting questions before they cover the work is a small, tangible and oversimplified tool. Still, it is the beginning of the process of learning to deal with the discomfort of uncertainty and building the tools and confidence to use whatever knowledge and skills they currently have to genuinely think about, break down and risk the start of a solution.

My coaching processes and Skills are designed on this basis. I scratch at the building blocks, unarticulated and underlying concepts and skills required to develop professional skills and provide simple and tangible tools to help students begin developing these skills. Thus, the tools may not initially appear to be related to professional skills in the form they are discussed in curriculum development. They may be perceived as oversimplified and inappropriate for the levels required in professional qualification exams.

body: This is a recording of a webinar I ran with students who were starting their preparation for a Board Exam. (Context below the video)

While the context will explain the students' levels in this particular session, the content illustrates the explicit explanation of the 'past' vs. the 'future' in terms of how students study and what they believe the exams require of them.
The main underlying message of this session was: Do you realise that the difference between your past and your current and future exams is NOT about the difficulty and volumes of knowledge?
Components of this discussion:
The changes between the past and future (0:00 - 19:00)
Same knowledge, different skill requirements (19:14)
Skills need to be 'owned' (23:50)
The Skill of solving new problems - Uncertainty (25:10)
This session was for students who were starting to prepare for SAICA's Initial Assessment of Competence (IAC). This is the first Board Exam for the South African Chartered Accountant qualification.
These students have passed a postgraduate qualification (CTA / PGDA).
The APC exam I refer to is the second and last Board Exam that they will write - The Assessment of Professional Competence.
This particular session was held in 2024, where the pass rates for the recent IAC exam were concerningly low, and the average pass rate for the APC over the previous few years was around 60%.

lessons.title: Goal orientation
body: Mindset research suggests that fixed'ers are more likely to lean towards performance goal orientation (the belief that the purpose of studying is to get the answer right) as opposed to a learning goal orientation (the belief that the purpose of studying is to learn, and the inherent awareness that this is a cumulative process that takes time).

If we have fixed'er students in our classes, their focus is on getting the answer right. Their studying will be spent on theory with the belief that if they have enough theory, they will pass the questions. If they're not passing practice questions, obviously, their studying has 'failed'. They may spend the same hours as growth'ers in their studying, but they are not focussing on the same skills.
The survey feedback on students' reluctance to do questions...

lessons.title: Effort beliefs
body: 'Effort' - We need to know 'What type...' rather than 'How much...?'

Research may explore the hours that students are investing in their studies, but this does not reflect the type of studying they are focussing on. Based on the discussion above, a student who focusses on memory in earlier levels may spend as many hours, and even more, studying the same way in higher levels, with less and less effectiveness. We need to know whether they have shifted their study approaches to match the skill requirements at higher levels.

When we ask students about the 'effort' they invest in their studies, (assuming they answer completely honestly), are we referring to the same 'effort'? Students may be referring to hours and memory, while we may be referring to the time they invest in skill development.
Mashishi and Rabin's (2000) findings highlight the importance of exploring the type of effort students are investing.

lessons.title: What do i mean by learned helplessness in this context
body: Def: Learned helplessness occurs when an individual continuously faces a negative, uncontrollable situation and stops trying to change their circumstances, even when they have the ability to do so.
In the context of my work with students, these are some of the behaviours and beliefs I come across that I believe are related to learned helplessness

Forgetting that they've successfully achieved academic goals in the past when they're facing a situation that they're struggling with. Their ability to learn is forgotten, and they feel helpless in the face of their struggle

Fear of attempting practice questions out of the concern about what it 'means' to get them wrong, along with the unconscious fear that their performance on the practice question will dictate the sum total of their abilities (ie: It will never get better than this)

Refusing to attempt questions with the belief that they shouldn't attempt to solve a problem if you don't have the entire solution and all the knowledge before you start. ie: "I'm not able to think about it myself. I have to be given all the knowledge first, for exactly this level of work and problem"

In terms of the structure of many accounting classes, and the nature of most accounting topics, it appears to make sense to provide knowledge first, since there's clearly a right and wrong answer. However, should this continue for too long, it can reasonably be expected to create a belief that learning has to start with knowledge first, and that the right / wrong nature of the work means that there's no point in trying to think of anything yourself.
In this section, I share some content and thoughts related to this.

lessons.title: Excerpt why should i do questions first
body: This is an excerpt of a discussion I had with a student who was repeating third year.

He was spending a lot of time studying theory, trying to understand and master all the work before he 'felt ready' to do any questions. When he did get to questions, he found that even though he had felt he had understood the work, the questions were still not making sense and he still wasn't able to answer the questions.

My advice to students is to start their studying with questions, and to shift their belief in the purpose of questions from "Am I ready to pass?" to a more effective way to guide their learning, and develop an awareness of skills other than knowledge that they need to work on (more than two weeks before their exams).

lessons.title: Failure trigger
body: Not all failures are failure triggers, and not all failure triggers are failures

A 'Failure Trigger' is a unique type of experience that challenges a student’s mindset in a fundamental way. Unlike ordinary setbacks or obstacles, a failure trigger represents a deeper, more personal encounter with failure—something that shakes a student’s confidence to its core.

This concept goes beyond simply encountering difficulty or making mistakes. A failure trigger is often a situation that feels insurmountable, even with effort, and may evoke self-doubt about one's abilities. Importantly, it’s not necessarily any failure but rather a specific type of failure or challenge that a student perceives as a 'wall' as opposed to an 'obstacle'.
Obstacles vs Walls: Defining the Difference
To clarify the distinction, you describe two types of challenges: obstacles and walls.

Obstacles are setbacks that, while challenging, appear manageable. The student may struggle, but they can still see a way to overcome them, even if it requires more effort or adjustment. For example, a student might fail a subject due to insufficient preparation, missing classes, or other distractions. They feel disappointed but understand that they could succeed by attending more classes or studying more consistently. In this case, the challenge is tangible and solvable—something they can see past and adjust their behaviour to achieve. The student retains a sense of control and can use problem-solving to improve, which aligns with a growth mindset perspective.

Walls, on the other hand, are perceived as unbreakable barriers that the student cannot see past. When facing a wall, a student may feel completely out of their depth, unable to identify a way forward, and uncertain if success is even possible. For instance, a student may feel that their previous strategies and efforts are no longer effective to pass an exam or subject, leading to a sense of being lost or overwhelmed. They may increase their study time and effort, only to find that the material or difficulty level remains insurmountable. They may feel that their usual approaches no longer work, leaving them feeling helpless and questioning their capabilities.

Obstacle Example: A student might miss a few classes or be distracted by personal issues, resulting in poor performance on an exam. Although disappointed, they can pinpoint the reasons for their setback, such as lack of preparation, and recognize how they could do better by adjusting their approach, like studying more thoroughly or seeking extra help. Here, they retain a growth-oriented outlook because they see the failure as something within their control to improve upon.

Wall Example: In contrast, a student may find themselves in a situation where they feel their previous academic strategies fail them. Even after doubling their efforts, attending all classes, and trying harder than ever, they find themselves lost and unable to make sense of the material. They may not even know what kind of help to ask for. This sense of hitting a wall can evoke a fixed mindset response, where they might conclude, "Maybe I’m just not smart enough," or, "Perhaps I’m not cut out for this program."

Failure Trigger in Real Student Experiences: One student, for instance, discovered after a full year of study that her program was not accredited, meaning she would need to redo the year to pursue her academic goals. Despite the setback, she used this experience as a resilience-building moment. However, when faced with the demands of the final year of her accounting degree, she found herself questioning her intellectual capabilities. This shift exposed a more fixed mindset under the pressure of this unmanageable wall. This particular example is also a valuable reflection of the disconnect between students' conscious and unconscious beliefs and processes.

Failure Trigger and Mindset The Failure Trigger serves as a pivotal moment where students' underlying mindsets surface most clearly. Those with a growth mindset may interpret the Failure Trigger as an extreme but surmountable challenge, prompting them to search for new strategies or resources to overcome it. However, students with a fixed mindset might see it as a reflection of their innate limitations, concluding they lack the talent or intelligence needed for success.

Summary In essence, a Failure Trigger is not just any failure; it’s a moment that forces students to confront their deepest beliefs about their abilities. When students encounter a wall—a seemingly insurmountable barrier—they often reveal whether they hold a fixed or growth mindset. The Failure Trigger thus becomes a unique window into understanding how students respond to their hardest challenges, particularly in high-stakes academic environments.

lessons.title: Strategic study focus results vs process
body: Accounting students can often be more focussed on the right answer, than the process that should be applied to arrive at the answer. They are generally not aware of the difference in focus here. If they are performance goal oriented, they are predominantly focussed on being right, and their perception would be that if you get the right answer, it means that you already have the right process. This perception is increasingly problematic at higher levels where problems are more subjective, require professional judgement, and require a process of breaking down the problem and building a solution.

lessons.title: Do you like the subject or the feeling of achieving
body: (Needs to be re-recorded)

Students connect their emotions to subjects, without necessarily realising that it may not be the subject matter they're connecting with. In a lot of cases, especially for students who lean towards a fixed mindset, they enjoy the feeling of achievement and intelligence validation. It doesn't matter what the subject is, because the purpose of studying is not learning, it's achieving. This means that students may 'enjoy' subjects at earlier levels and then develop a dislike for them later. The subject hasn't changed, but their performance has. They don't like the feeling of not doing well, and unconsciously connect that to the subject-matter instead of the feeling of achievement they crave.

lessons.title: What i want you to know about feeling stupid
Practical development of skills
body: I provide practical tools that are simple enough to apply to their next study session. While they are oversimplified versions of the skills required - communication, application, systematic and critical thinking - the tools provide the first, and most importantly, tangible step in moving from 'here' to 'there'. Students often see solutions to questions that require higher levels of professional skills and can acknowledge the gap between their current abilities and what will be expected of them, they have no tangible process to start developing these skills.

If students have passed previous exams based on pattern recognition, problem matching, and the filing cabinet approach, their solution to this problem is often to build a database of ideal solutions to these types of questions - Their next solution will look like the last solution. When they find changes, they add this to the database of ideal answers. They can create highly sophisticated databases with lots of 'exceptions' and 'if this... then that', but this is still memory-based learning.

These are scaffolds, the stepping stone to start the process. Once the student has overcome the intimidation of a new skill and, very importantly, can see they have made even a small amount of progress in the right direction, this is generally enough to help them continue to practice and apply this skill. As they develop this skill, they leave the scaffold behind. The simplicity of the tools I provide are not enough for them to pass high-level professional requirements, but they are simple enough to start the skill development with less resistance and intimidation.
